questions.q: Why push work like email sending onto a background queue instead of doing it in the request?
options: Queues guarantee each email is delivered exactly once to recipients
The request returns quickly while slow, retryable work happens async
Background workers are exempt from provider rate limits
SMTP connections require a dedicated long-lived process anyway

questions.q: At-least-once delivery means job handlers must be...
options: idempotent, because the same job can arrive more than once
acknowledged before any processing work begins
strictly ordered by their enqueue timestamps
stateless, holding no data whatsoever between successive executions

questions.q: A job fails with a transient network timeout. Standard first response?
options: Move it directly to the dead-letter queue for manual review
Drop it and rely on the producer to resend eventually
Halt the entire queue until an operator investigates
Retry it with exponential backoff and jitter

questions.q: A malformed job crashes its worker on every attempt and keeps getting redelivered. This is called...
options: a zombie job
a tombstone message
a poison message
a livelocked consumer

questions.q: Why acknowledge a message only after processing finishes?
options: A worker crash mid-job then causes redelivery instead of loss
It keeps the consumer's committed offset strictly monotonic
Brokers require late acknowledgments to preserve FIFO ordering
Late acks reduce network chatter between polling cycles

questions.q: What is a dead-letter queue for?
options: Buffering in-flight messages while the broker restarts
Holding low-priority jobs until off-peak hours arrive
Replicating critical jobs across availability zones
Parking jobs that exhausted retries, for inspection and replay

questions.q: Why add jitter to retry backoff delays?
options: To randomize job priorities so no single tenant starves
To keep each retry pinned to its original worker
To desynchronize retry storms hammering a recovering dependency
To make retry timestamps unique for distributed tracing

questions.q: Where should a large video live when you enqueue a transcoding job?
options: Inline in the message body, base64-encoded for transport safety
In object storage, with the message carrying only a reference
On the producing server's local disk until a worker connects back
Split across a numbered sequence of chunked messages

questions.q: A service enqueues 'send confirmation' inside a DB transaction that later rolls back, but the message was already published. Fix?
options: Use a transactional outbox so publish happens only after commit
Rely on the broker to garbage-collect messages for missing orders
Publish before opening the transaction so ordering is preserved
Have consumers ignore messages older than the transaction timeout

questions.q: With the outbox pattern, how do events actually reach the broker?
options: A commit hook publishes them synchronously inside the transaction
The broker polls an HTTP endpoint the application exposes
A relay (poller or CDC) reads committed outbox rows and publishes them
Consumers query the outbox table directly instead of subscribing to a broker

questions.q: A worker charges a card, then crashes before acking. The message is redelivered. What prevents double billing?
options: The broker suppresses redelivery once side effects are detected
An idempotency key so the payment provider dedupes the charge
At-least-once semantics, which only ever duplicate reads, never writes
The card network's automatic same-amount deduplication window

questions.q: Queue depth grows steadily while workers run at 100% utilization. What is the real lever?
options: Increase message TTL so nothing expires while queued
Switch dequeueing from FIFO to LIFO ordering
Compress payloads so the backlog drains faster
Add consumers or cut per-job time; arrivals exceed service rate

questions.q: One tenant enqueues a million jobs, starving everyone on the shared queue. Best structural fix?
options: Raise the global queue size limit substantially
Sort the whole queue by enqueue timestamp instead of priority
Per-tenant queues or weighted fair dequeueing across tenants
Have workers skip any batch larger than a threshold

questions.q: After scheduler failover, two schedulers fire the same nightly job. What prevents double execution?
options: A unique run-key claim (lock) that only one instance can win
Tight NTP clock synchronization between the scheduler hosts
Staggering the schedule to a less contended time window
The queue's FIFO ordering guarantee on message delivery

questions.q: Which failure should NOT be retried automatically?
options: An HTTP 503 from a downstream dependency
A network timeout while talking to the database
A deadlock-victim error returned by the database
A validation error proving the payload can never succeed

questions.q: A job's processing time exceeds the queue's visibility timeout. What happens?
options: The broker deletes the message as expired
It becomes visible again and another worker may process it concurrently
The broker keeps extending the timeout automatically until the worker completes
The ack fails and the job is instantly dead-lettered

questions.q: An outbox relay publishes, crashes before marking rows sent, then republishes on restart. Net delivery guarantee?
options: Exactly-once, since the outbox table itself is transactional
At-most-once, since unsent rows may be skipped on restart
Per-aggregate ordered delivery with duplicates fully suppressed
At-least-once; consumers still need idempotent handling

questions.q: 100k jobs fail together during a 10-minute dependency outage, all on fixed 30-second retry. What happens at recovery?
options: The backlog drains smoothly since queues absorb bursts by design
Synchronized retry waves can re-topple the dependency; add jitter and caps
All 100k jobs dead-letter simultaneously when the outage ends
Nothing notable; fixed intervals are self-desynchronizing over time

questions.q: You need each job's effect applied exactly once end-to-end over an at-least-once queue. What is achievable?
options: Effectively-once via idempotent handlers or dedup keys; transport stays at-least-once
True exactly-once, if broker acknowledgments are made transactional
Exactly-once, provided every consumer runs single-threaded
Exactly-once, whenever FIFO queues with dedup windows are used

questions.q: A job writes database state and calls an unrevertible external API. Sound approach?
options: Call the API first so the database only ever reflects reality
Span both operations in one distributed transaction with the provider
Commit state first, then call the API idempotently with retries and reconciliation
Interleave the two and lean on the queue's retry semantics
